The Casino Crown — Macau vs Las Vegas vs Singapore (2005–2026)

00:00 Intro — Why this race matters
00:38 2005–2010: Early boom (Macau breakout)
01:32 2011–2013: Macau’s meteoric peak
02:18 2014–2019: Plateau and competition
03:10 2020: The COVID collapse — shockwaves
04:05 2021–2024: Recovery trajectory
05:10 2025–2026: Outlook & projections (est.)
06:00 Outro & sources

Story in short: Between 2005 and 2013 Macau exploded from under $7B to more than $46B in annual gross gaming revenue (GGR), overtaking the Las Vegas Strip and changing global casino economics. Las Vegas grew steadily but never matched Macau’s run; Singapore built a premium niche with Marina Bay Sands and Resorts World Sentosa. Then 2020’s pandemic wiped out travel: Macau fell to roughly $3.6B (down ~90% from 2019), the Strip plunged to ~$1.95B, and Singapore nearly shut down. From 2021 onward the recovery is visible — but the market shape has changed.

instagram_caption:
🎲 Macau’s meteoric rise — and the crash that rewrote the casino map.

From 2005 to 2013 Macau’s annual gambling take exploded from about $6.7B to an eye-popping $46.3B — a leap that made Macau the planet’s casino capital and left traditional hubs scrambling. For context: the Las Vegas Strip in 2013 was roughly $7.1B and Singapore around $4.2B. Macau’s boom was driven by mainland China mass-market play and a flood of new integrated resorts.

Then the story flips. Between 2014–2019 Macau plateaued around the mid-$30s (billion USD) as anti-graft measures, regulatory shifts and changing Chinese travel patterns cooled the frenzy. The real cliff came in 2020: Macau’s GGR crashed to about $3.6B — a near-total shutdown. Las Vegas fell too (to ~$1.95B) and Singapore nearly paused (about $0.5B) as borders slammed shut.

Recovery began in fits and starts: 2021 shows a partial rebound (Macau ~$7.4B, Las Vegas ~$5.4B, Singapore ~$0.9B). By 2023 Macau regained momentum ($29.8B) and 2024 pushed further (~$34.5B). Las Vegas climbed back methodically (2024 est. $9.1B) and Singapore’s premium product recovered faster than expected (~$5.0B in 2024). My 2025–26 outlook (estimates) projects Macau at ~$37.5B (2025) and ~$40.0B (2026), Las Vegas to $9.8B / $10.5B, and Singapore to $5.6B / $6.2B as global travel normalizes and high-roller flows return.

This isn’t just numbers — it’s a tournament of geography, policy and tourism. Macau’s surge shows what happens when demand, regulation and capital align; the 2020 crash shows how fragile a travel-dependent economy can be. Las Vegas’s steadier climb shows diversification and domestic tourism resilience. Singapore carved a premium lane that proved more recession-resistant once borders reopened.

Which market do you think wins the next decade — Macau’s scale, Las Vegas’s resilience, or Singapore’s premium niche? Tell me why in the comments. Follow for the full chart-race video and dataset — tap follow to catch the animation and share if you want a downloadable CSV.
